title: A ripple tank with two dippers
alt: A shallow glass-floored tank of water on four legs. A bar across it holds two vibrators, each with a rod whose ball tip dips into the water. A red marker floats on the water.

scale.note: Ripples drawn higher and slower than they are.

parts.name: Glass floor
parts.note: light shone through it shows the ripples as bright and dark bands on a screen.

parts.name: Wall
parts.note: the sides slope inside in a real tank, so the waves do not bounce back into the pattern.

parts.name: Wall
parts.note: holds the water: about a centimetre deep.

parts.name: Legs
parts.note: hold the tank level, so the water is equally deep everywhere and the waves keep one speed.

parts.name: Upright
parts.note: holds the vibrators' bar over the water.

parts.name: Bar
parts.note: the vibrators slide along it: their distance apart is d.

parts.name: Vibrator 1
parts.note: a small motor with an off-centre weight: it shakes its rod up and down at a steady beat.

parts.name: Source S₁
parts.note: the ball dips into the water and lifts out again, once a beat: circular waves spread from it.

parts.name: Point P
parts.note: the point whose motion is worked out below the figure. Click the water to move it.

steps.title: One source
steps.text: Only S₁ is beating. Its waves spread out in circles, and grow smaller as they go: the same energy is spread round an ever longer circle.

steps.title: Two sources in step
steps.text: Both dippers beat together. Where a crest of one meets a crest of the other the water rises twice as high; where a crest meets a trough it stays nearly still.

steps.title: The point P
steps.text: Click the water to move P. The white lines are where the water stays still: there, S₂ is farther than S₁ by a whole number of wavelengths and a half.

steps.title: Out of step
steps.text: S₂ now goes down as S₁ goes up. Every line of still water and every line of large waves swaps places: the middle line, equally far from both, is now still.

steps.title: Shorter waves
steps.text: With shorter waves the lines crowd together: between the sources there are about 2d/λ of them. Seen here as a map of how much the water moves.
